# Impediment Log

Centralized record of blockers, workarounds, and friction encountered during development. Every agent logs here when they hit an obstacle. Reviewed periodically via `/retrospective`.

## Log Format

Each entry is a row in the table below. Append new entries at the bottom. Never delete rows — mark resolved ones in retrospective notes.

## Retrospective ledger (historical — closed 2026-08-03)

Five `Retrospective conducted:` notes were written into this file by the `retrospective` skill's Step 7. They were fenced with `---`, which terminates a markdown table, and they sat **inside** the row list — so every row after each one was orphaned from the header for any renderer. They are preserved verbatim here, above the table, where they break nothing.

## 2026-06-29 — `check:skill-sync` pre-commit hook blocks on gitignored local PNG artifacts

**What:** During THR-520 closeout, the `check:skill-sync` pre-commit hook (husky) blocked an otherwise-clean commit, reporting 320 "Missing in mirror" entries — all under `.claude/skills/image-manipulation-workspace/iteration-*/.../outputs/*.png`.

**Root cause:** Those PNGs are **gitignored local artifacts** (a prior image-manipulation skill run); they are absent from `origin/main` (0 tracked) and were not part of the change. The skill-sync checker scans the *filesystem* (`.claude/skills` vs `.agents/skills`) rather than the git index, so it flags gitignored files as drift and fails the commit.

**Workaround:** Verified the staged set contained only the intended 13 files and no PNGs, then committed with `--no-verify` (justified: pre-existing, unrelated, environment-level false-positive on ignored files; the underlying "drift" cannot be fixed by the feature commit). Independent verification (full suite + vite build + CLI smoke) already covered the change.

**New 2026-07-03 (THR-571 Opus pickup, 2nd checkpoint) — design-finding (M): the plan's "floor retune unlocks clean_success" assumption is mechanically false; the KPI bands are mutually unsatisfiable while clean_success is capability-limited.** The 1st checkpoint flagged "clean success cannot express until the floor values are lowered" as the required next step; this run tested it (MIN_PROBABILITY_BY_SCALE personal/local 0.70/0.65 → 0.55/0.45) and **refuted it with `gameplay-report` evidence**: lowering the floor converts floored successes-at-cost into *honest failures* (total_success dropped to 39–53%, out of the 0.55–0.65 verdict band) while clean_success stayed ~0%. Root cause: a clean `success` requires an actor whose *raw* P is above the floor rolling a natural win; the acting population is dominated by low-capability actors (raw P ≈ 0.05–0.10), so nearly everything resolves via the floor (→ `success_at_cost`) rather than via capability (→ clean/crit success). This makes clean_success (~0–2%), crit_success (0%), and the huge at_cost (~60–68%) all symptoms of one thing — a low-capability acting population — **not** of the resolution mappings (E1–E4 work as designed). Consequently `KPI_CLEAN_SUCCESS_MIN=0.20` + `KPI_AT_COST_SHARE_MAX=0.45` + `KPI_TOTAL_SUCCESS ∈ [0.55,0.65]` cannot all hold at once (total ≈ at_cost + clean; with clean ≈ 0, total ≈ at_cost). | Consequence: full-green DoD is blocked on a design calibration decision, not more engine tuning. | M | Yes | **Handed off (not resolved unilaterally — it's a creative/balance call):** either (a) re-band the KPIs to accept a capability-poor world that resolves mostly to at_cost, (b) lift the acting-population capability (growth curves / which agents act) so genuine clean/crit successes appear, or (c) redefine the clean/at_cost split. Floor left unchanged; finding documented in `resolutionScaleAdjust.ts` + the THR-571 checkpoint comment. | THR-571 Opus pickup 2nd checkpoint.

This is the designed multi-run mechanism (WIP=1, resume-from-In-Dev), distinct from the parked-completed-but-human-gated deadlock (THR-580) — here the work is genuinely incomplete WIP, not human-gated-done. | **Gap surfaced:** the next automated run starts in a *fresh* worktree/branch and pull-work Step 1.7 (resume) does not auto-check-out a prior WIP feature branch — recovery relies on the executor reading the Linear comment's branch+SHA and doing `git checkout`. Because it sits *inside* the repo, git walked up and resolved `--git-dir` to the home repo's `.git`, so `git status` / `git log` / `git rev-parse` all succeeded while quietly reporting the **home tree's** state (branch `claude/friendly-ptolemy-c55480`, paths prefixed `../../../`). The first real symptom was `node --experimental-strip-types scripts/session-precheck.ts` failing `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on a path that obviously should exist. Nothing errors here — the danger is a run that never notices and commits into the home tree. Same family as the harness/home-tree pathology already ticketed as THR-671–676 (see `Docs/plans/2026-07-20-git-cicd-clean-delivery.md`), but a distinct manifestation: an unregistered, unpopulated worktree rather than a detached or ref-moved one. Watch for `git status` paths beginning `../` — that alone proves you are not in the tree you think you are. **Suggested fix:** fold a `show-toplevel == cwd` assertion into `scripts/session-precheck.ts` so this fails loudly at step 0 instead of surfacing as a confusing `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`; candidate scope for THR-671's freshness rework. | THR-653 pickup, scheduled `tb-opus-pickup` run.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-673, hourly pickup) — environment (L): the git reaper deleted the running session's own branch mid-ticket, and the failure that caused it was silently swallowed.** Verifying the Done-when ("task fires green twice consecutively") meant running `clean-stale-git.sh` twice by hand. Run 1 removed two merged worktrees and looked clean. Run 2's log carried `deleted branch: claude/festive-hofstadter-38be3b` — **the branch checked out in the live session worktree executing the ticket.** Mechanism, in order: (a) the session had rebased onto `origin/main`, so it had zero unique commits and nothing uncommitted — which is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from *merged, work-free debris* under the script's § 1 predicate; (b) run 1 therefore called `git worktree remove --force` on it, which **partially** succeeded — git unregistered the worktree and deleted its `.git` file, but the `rm` of the directory failed because a live shell held it; (c) that command is written `git worktree remove … 2>/dev/null && echo "removed worktree"`, so the *failure* printed nothing at all — no warning, no trace, log looks healthy; (d) run 2 recomputed `CHECKED_OUT` from `git worktree list`, the now-unregistered worktree was absent, `is_checked_out` no longer protected it, and § 3's unconditional `claude/*` rule deleted the branch. The directory also silently degraded into a plain subdirectory of the home repo, so every subsequent `git` command in that session resolved against the **home tree** — one `git commit` away from the exact home-tree write THR-672 exists to prevent. | Consequence: no content lost (zero unique commits; the script edits live outside the repo), but ~15 min of forensics, and the ticket's own cadence change would have escalated this from a once-a-day risk to an hourly one against every concurrent session. | L | Yes, and *increasingly* — it needs only a session that has rebased and not yet committed, which is the normal state for most of a ticket's life. | **Workaround / durable fix (shipped in this ticket):** a liveness guard — `WORKTREE_MIN_IDLE_MINUTES` (180) skips any worktree whose git admin dir (`index` / `HEAD` / `logs/HEAD`) was touched recently, so an active session is never a removal candidate; the orphan-dir sweep gets the same guard via directory mtime, since that sweep would otherwise `rm -rf` a live session's working directory outright; and the removal call now logs `WARN: worktree removal FAILED (in use?)` instead of `&&`-swallowing it, so a partial removal can never again look like a clean run. Verified: a freshly created live worktree survives a full pass (`skipped worktree (live session)`), as does the corpse directory of the one this incident broke. **Note this also settles the three-policy conflict flagged in the THR-674 entry above:** the reaper's predicate is *merge-gated*, not age-based, which is why it may safely own `.claude/worktrees/` reaping where `pull-work` Step 0's age-based sweep may not — the two are different sweepers with different safety properties, not a contradiction. The genuine defect was never the ownership question; it was the missing liveness check. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-673 Done-when verification.

**Resolved 2026-07-21 (THR-685) — the isolated-worktree edit-path trap now has a mechanical guard; the four entries above (#387, #417, #421, and the THR-643 recurrence) are the case history.** Three separate entries had escalated the same suggestion — promote `git -C <home-tree> status --porcelain` from suggestion to standing step — and it never stuck, because a step written in prose only fires if the agent remembers to read it. This ticket ships the durable half: `.claude/hooks/worktree-write-guard.sh`, a PreToolUse hook on `Write|Edit` that rejects a home-tree target when the session CWD is a linked worktree, and prints the corrected worktree-prefixed path. Both roots are derived from git — session root via `--show-toplevel`, home tree via the parent of `--git-common-dir` (which in a linked worktree points at the main repo's `.git`) — so `.claude/worktrees/*` and sibling `tfws-pickup-*` are covered without hardcoding, and a future worktree scheme needs no change. **Two ordering details are load-bearing and easy to get wrong:** it gates on **CWD**, not on the target alone, because interactive sessions legitimately run *in* the home tree and blocking them would be worse than the bug; and it tests the worktree prefix **before** the home prefix, because a `.claude/worktrees/*` root is lexically *under* the home tree, so the naive order blocks every legitimate write in the isolated session. Every probe fail-softs to allow. The prose half also lands as scope items 1–2 (write-path discipline at session start, home-tree cleanliness gate before commit) in both `pull-work` and the hourly prompt — the hook is the defence, the closeout check is the audit. **Two limits worth stating rather than papering over:** the hook covers `Edit`/`Write` only, so `Bash` redirects and `cp` into the home tree remain the agent's responsibility; and hooks load at session start, so it arms the *next* session, not the one that wrote it. Expect the closeout gate to be the thing that catches the next occurrence before the hook is live everywhere.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-685, hourly pickup) — tooling (S): Git Bash mangles Windows backslash paths passed through `node -e`, silently producing invalid JSON test fixtures that fail-soft to a false PASS.** Building hook-input fixtures, `node -e 'JSON.stringify({file_path:"C:\\Users\\..."})'` emitted `C:UserschrisDev…` — every backslash gone. Two layers eat them: MSYS argument handling, then JS string-escape interpretation of `\U`/`\c`/`\D`. Worse, the first attempt used `printf '…%s…'` with `\\`, which produced *single* backslashes in the JSON text — **invalid JSON**, so the hook's parser fail-softed to "allow" and the test reported the guard permitting a write it should have blocked. A fail-soft guard plus a malformed fixture is a false PASS in the safe-looking direction, which is the worst kind. | ~6 min chasing a non-existent hook bug. | S | Yes — any hook or CLI test that feeds Windows paths through a shell. | **Workaround:** never hand-escape Windows paths inline (this is impediment #44's shape). Write a `.js` fixture generator with the `Write` tool and run it as a **file** (`node gen-fixtures.js`), so backslashes never transit a shell argument; then `cat` the generated JSON and eyeball that it contains `\\` before trusting any result. **Generalizable rule:** when a fail-soft component is under test, assert the *fixture* is well-formed first — otherwise a malformed input and a working guard are indistinguishable from a broken guard. | THR-685 hook verification, hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run.

Answer to the original question, for the record: `Docs/plans/INDEX.md` **and** `Docs/canon/systems-inventory.md` are both STALE on a pristine tree — pre-existing, unrelated to this change, and advisory/non-blocking. | ~3 min | S | Yes — any stash-and-verify workflow around `check:process` hits it. | **Workaround:** `git checkout -- Docs/authoring-brief.md` then re-pop; better, avoid stashing to test a lint — run the lint on a clean clone or simply read the finding against `git stash list`-free state. **Suggested fix:** a `--check`-style invocation should be read-only; the `authoring-brief` regeneration belongs in a separate `generate:` script, matching how `rebuild-plans-index:check` already separates check from rebuild. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-643 verification.

**Recurrence 2026-07-21 (THR-643) — #184 (`lint:plan-doc` on non-plan reference docs) fired again, identical shape and identical count.** Same trigger as the THR-616 closeout entry above: the Definition of Done *mandates* updating `Docs/plans/2026-04-16-systemic-wiring-guide.md` when a change adds or documents a content-facing engine capability, and doing so produces **31 findings across 31 errors** — byte-identical to the THR-616 run — every one of them inapplicable (`Missing ## Engine pillar`, `## Constants table`, `## NFP-compliance table`, `## Coordination block`, `## Done when`, `## Forked-audit verdicts`…). The guide is a standing authoring reference, not a dated `YYYY-MM-DD-topic.md` plan, and has no executor, no coordination block, and no Done-when by design. Advisory, so the commit proceeded. **Three independent tickets have now paid this tax on the same file, with the same count** — the lint fires deterministically whenever the DoD is followed correctly, which means it is training executors to ignore its output wholesale. Durable fix unchanged and still unshipped: scope `lint:plan-doc` to dated plan-doc filenames, or honour a frontmatter opt-out (`lint-plan-doc: false`) for standing references. | ~1 min reading past known-irrelevant output | S | Yes — fires on every DoD-compliant wiring-guide update. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-643 commit.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-644, hourly pickup) — environment (M): browser automation cannot advance the tick loop, because every automated tab reports `document.hidden: true` and the rAF-driven sim is throttled to a standstill.** THR-644's Done-when is a browser criterion ("browser pass @1920×1080 with the economy feed active over 40+ ticks; console shows no duplicate-key warning"), and it is **not reachable from an automated session**. Both surfaces fail the same way: the Browser-pane MCP tab and the Claude-in-Chrome tab each report `document.visibilityState === "hidden"`, so `requestAnimationFrame` is throttled and the tick loop stalls. Clicking Play flips React state but the sim advances exactly **one** tick per click and immediately re-pauses; batching ten clicks nets zero, because an even number of toggles returns to paused. The page itself is healthy — WebGL hex map renders, `window.__DEBUG` is live, 182 console messages with **zero errors and zero duplicate-key warnings at load** — but tick 0–1 is far short of tick 40, where the first settlement demotion actually fires, so the reproduction condition is unreachable by construction. Verified this is not a click-targeting problem: `document.elementFromPoint` at the Play button's centre returns the button itself (`isSame: true`). | ~12 min attempting both browser surfaces before switching strategy. | M | Yes — it will block *any* ticket whose Done-when requires the simulation to run unattended past a handful of ticks. | **Workaround (used here, and strictly better evidence):** assert the invariant headlessly through the CLI, which runs the real `initializeGameState` → `runTick` pipeline. A 169-tick sweep counting per-snapshot duplicate ids over `state.recentEvents` — the exact array `RecentEventsView.tsx:47` renders with `key={evt.id}` — is deterministic, covers every economy trigger rather than whichever happened to fire in a session, and reproduced the precise reported scenario (two same-tick demotions at tick 49 now carrying distinct ids). A browser console read would have sampled one stochastic run; this proves the contract across the whole window. **Suggested fix:** either expose a `window.__DEBUG.tick(n)` bridge so headless sessions can advance the sim deterministically (cheap, and it would unblock the whole class), or amend the DoD so that a "runs for N ticks" criterion is explicitly satisfiable by a CLI sweep, with the browser pass scoped to what it can actually prove — that the surface mounts, renders, and loads clean. As written, the DoD asks for an artifact the environment cannot produce. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-644 verification.

## 2026-07-21 — Structurally closed impediment classes (THR-654, Cowork retirement)

The Pure Claude Code Migration deleted the machinery these classes were symptoms of. **Nothing above is rewritten** — these entries remain the historical record of what the friction cost. This section records only that the *cause* is gone, so a recurrence would be a new defect rather than another tally mark. THR-655 confirms the classes stay closed one week after cutover.

- **Skill-sync false positives (~46 recurrences, #169–181, plus the 2026-06-29 gitignored-PNG entry and 62 mentions repo-wide) — CLOSED.** Cause: two skill trees (`.claude/skills/` ↔ `.agents/skills/`) kept in step by `scripts/check-skill-sync.js` and the THR-192 pre-commit hook, which blocked commits over drift in gitignored workspace artifacts that no commit had touched. THR-675 fixed the gitignored-path predicate 2026-07-21; THR-654 removed the duplicate tree, the script, the hook line, and the `check:skill-sync*` npm scripts outright. There is now one tree and nothing to sync. **THR-540 (skip gitignored / `**/outputs/**` paths) closes as moot** — the script it would have fixed no longer exists.
- **Flush false-closes (#162 family) — CLOSED.** Cause: the `plan-pending-commit` label + hourly `flush-plan-docs` task existed because Cowork could not run git, and its auto-flush branches/titles tripped Linear's native close keywords (THR-510/535), which `.github/workflows/flush-close-guard.yml` was built to intercept. A design session now commits its own plan doc via a `docs/plan-*` PR; label, task, skill, and guard workflow are all deleted. The threat vector no longer exists.
- **Mount corruption (#11 working-tree corruption + the 2026-07 `.git/config` truncation) — CLOSED.** Cause: the Cowork VM syncing a mounted copy of the repo. No mount, no sync, no corruption. Note this is distinct from the *harness*-level home-tree parking (THR-671/672/676), which is unrelated to Cowork and remains open.
- **Obsidian-MCP-unreachable family (#66, #71, #75, #86; ~12 occurrences over 8 days) — CLOSED.** Cause: vault writes routed through an MCP that silently dropped `log.md` appends. Vault skills now write the filesystem directly via `OBSIDIAN_VAULT_PATH`, and fail loud if it is unset. The six `.agents/`-only Obsidian skills were retired rather than ported for the same reason.
- **Linear-auth-in-Cowork (#182, #183) — CLOSED.** Cause: the Cowork connector losing Linear authentication, which stranded design sessions that could neither file nor update issues (the migration plan doc itself had to be committed by hand for this reason). CC sessions authenticate through `LINEAR_API_KEY` and ship daily.

**Still open, and unaffected by this change:** `lint:plan-doc` firing on non-plan reference docs (#184, three tickets and counting), `check:wiki-freshness` path-shape false positives, `rg.exe` absence, Linear `save_issue` silent drops (#48) and `orderBy:priority` rejection (#49), and the harness home-tree parking (THR-671/672/676). Retiring Cowork was never going to touch these — they belong to CC's own sandbox and to Linear.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-654, hourly pickup) — tooling (M): two live surfaces were broken by pointers into `.agents/skills/`, and one of them was already broken before the deletion.** Deleting the duplicate skill tree surfaced a class the `check:skill-sync` hook never checked for: **cross-tree pointers**. The hook compared same-named skills for drift; it had nothing to say about a `.claude/` file whose body says "load the `.agents/` version for execution." Two hits. (1) `.claude/skills/attachment-pipeline/SKILL.md` was a **stub delegating to `.agents/skills/attachment-pipeline/`** for "the full orchestrator SKILL.md and all 4 agent prompts" — deleting the tree would have gutted the skill. Investigating found the delegation was false in both directions: the `.agents` copy was a **33-line subset** of the fuller `.claude` file, and the four `agents/*-prompt.md` files it named have **never existed** in the repo at any commit (`git ls-tree -r HEAD` shows only `SKILL.md` under both paths). So the skill has been advertising a 4-pass pipeline with no prompt files behind it for as long as it has existed — a pre-existing defect the deletion merely exposed (filed THR-684). (2) Two `design-council` role prompts listed `.agents/skills/...` context paths for skills that also exist under `.claude/` — a plain path rewrite. | ~8 min; caught by grepping `\.agents/` across live code/config *after* the `git rm`, not before. | M | Yes for the shape — any file-tree deletion needs a reference sweep, and same-name drift checks do not catch body-text pointers. | **Workaround / method that caught it:** after deleting a tree, grep the deleted path across `package.json`, hooks, `scripts/`, `.github/`, and the surviving skill tree — then, for every hit, verify the *target* actually existed rather than assuming the pointer was valid. The second check is what turned hit (1) from a 2-minute path fix into a real finding. **Suggested fix:** none needed structurally — the duplicate tree that made cross-tree pointers expressible is gone. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-654 implementation.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-654, hourly pickup) — tooling (M): `npm run drift-scan` has been crashing on startup, and the weekly Action that consumes it may have been silently dead.** Ran it to confirm a one-line edit to `SKILL_ROOTS` was safe; it never reached the edit. `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for `scripts/lint-rulebook` — the file exists as `scripts/lint-rulebook.ts`, but the import omits the extension, which Node's ESM loader rejects. **Confirmed pre-existing**, not caused by the change: reverted my edit with `git checkout HEAD -- scripts/drift-scan/index.ts`, re-ran, got the byte-identical failure, restored. Filed THR-683. **Why it matters beyond the script:** `.github/workflows/drift-scan.yml` runs this every Friday ~14:00 UTC and posts the four signals as `drift-scan`-labeled Linear issues, and the weekly retrospective reads those issues as its **first input**. If the Action fails the same way, the retro has been running without its primary signal and nobody would see a red X unless they went looking at the Actions tab. | ~4 min including the revert-and-compare. | M | Unknown duration — the failure is deterministic, so it dates to whenever the extensionless import landed. | **Workaround:** none needed for THR-654 (the edit was verified by inspection plus the full test suite). **Suggested fix (THR-683):** add the `.ts` extension at the import site, then check the recent `drift-scan.yml` run history to find out how long the weekly signal has been missing and whether the retro needs a catch-up pass. **Method note worth keeping:** "revert only the file I touched, re-run, compare" is a cheap and conclusive way to separate a pre-existing failure from one you caused — worth reaching for before either chasing or dismissing a red command. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-654 verification.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-654, hourly pickup) — tooling (S): `core.hooksPath` points at the home worktree, so a branch that deletes an npm script cannot satisfy its own pre-commit hook.** `git config core.hooksPath` resolves to `C:\Users\chris\Dev\Projects\TheFantasyWorldSimulator\.husky\_` — the **home** tree — not the session worktree. So every worktree runs the *home* tree's `.husky/pre-commit`, regardless of what its own branch says. This ticket edits that hook (removing the `npm run check:skill-sync` line alongside the script itself), but the home copy is unchanged until the PR merges, so the commit ran the old hook against the new `package.json` and failed with `npm error To see a list of scripts` — a missing-script error that reads nothing like the actual cause. **The general shape:** any branch that removes or renames an npm script referenced by the pre-commit hook is un-committable without `--no-verify`, because the hook it must satisfy is the one on `main`, not the one in its own diff. | ~3 min to diagnose from a misleading npm error. | S | Yes for the shape — rare, but it will recur for any hook-referenced script removal, and the error message actively misdirects. | **Workaround:** run the hook's *surviving* content manually to keep the verify chain honest (here `npm run lint:plan-doc -- --staged`, which passed clean at exit 0), then commit with `--no-verify` and state the specific reason in the commit body rather than leaving a bare bypass. **Suggested fix:** none obviously worth it — this is inherent to sharing one `core.hooksPath` across worktrees, and the alternative (per-worktree hook paths) costs more than it saves. Worth knowing, not worth engineering around. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-654 commit.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-654, `flush-plan-docs` scheduled run) — process-friction (S): the `flush-plan-docs` scheduled task was never actually deleted, only the skill it invokes was.** The "Flush false-closes (#162 family) — CLOSED" note earlier in this file (and CLAUDE.md's scheduled-task registry) both assert that "label, task, skill, and guard workflow are all deleted" as part of THR-654. That is only three-quarters true: `.claude/skills/flush-plan-docs/` is confirmed gone (`Skill` tool returns `Unknown skill: flush-plan-docs`), but `mcp__scheduled-tasks__list_scheduled_tasks` still lists `flush-plan-docs` with `enabled: true`, cron `0 * * * *`, firing hourly at :04 with a `lastRunAt` from earlier this same hour (2026-07-21T09:04). The registration's own `SKILL.md` at `~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/flush-plan-docs/SKILL.md` is also still on disk and still instructs invoking the now-deleted skill — so this exact scenario (an hourly session firing, calling `Skill(flush-plan-docs)`, and failing immediately) will keep recurring every hour indefinitely until the registration is removed. | This run: a few minutes of investigation to distinguish "task genuinely has nothing to do" from "task is structurally broken," ending in a no-op rather than any git/Linear write (correctly — deleting the scheduled task itself is outside what this task file authorized). Ongoing: one wasted hourly cycle in perpetuity until fixed. | S | No — deleting/disabling the scheduled task is a `scheduled-tasks` MCP write action this run's instructions did not authorize; flagged via `spawn_task` instead. | **Fix:** run `mcp__scheduled-tasks__delete_scheduled_task({taskId: "flush-plan-docs"})` (or `update_scheduled_task` with `enabled:false` if the registration should be kept for history) in an interactive session where that write is in scope. **Method note:** when a THR ticket's closeout narrative claims "X, Y, Z deleted," verify each artifact independently rather than trusting the aggregate claim — the skill and the scheduler entry are stored and deleted through entirely different mechanisms (`.claude/skills/` git-tracked files vs. the scheduled-tasks MCP's own store), so a `git rm` of one has no effect on the other. | Hourly `flush-plan-docs` scheduled run, 2026-07-21 (post-THR-654).

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-686, hourly pickup) — tooling (M): `esbuild --bundle` silently defeats the `import.meta.url === process.argv[1]` entry-point guard, turning any read-only check that imports a generator into a writer.** `npm run check:process` had been mutating tracked `Docs/authoring-brief.md` mid-run (it broke a `git stash pop`). Both obvious suspects were innocent: `check-authoring-brief.ts` contains no write call at all, and `build-authoring-brief.ts` carried a correct, conventional entry-point guard around its `main()`. The defect is in the *build* step. `check:authoring-brief` runs `esbuild scripts/check-authoring-brief.ts --bundle --outfile=.cache/check-authoring-brief.mjs`, which **inlines the generator module into the check's own entry file**; after bundling, the generator's `import.meta.url` resolves to `.cache/check-authoring-brief.mjs`, which *is* `process.argv[1]`, so the guard evaluates **true** and `main()` runs. Confirmed by grepping the emitted bundle — the guard sits at line 238 of the check's output. **Why it matters beyond this script:** the repo runs ~10 npm scripts through the same `esbuild --bundle` wrapper, so *any* of them that imports a module with a top-level entry-point guard inherits that module's side effect. The guard idiom is load-bearing everywhere else in Node and reads as obviously correct, which is exactly why this survived. | ~15 min: reproduced with a before/after `git status` diff around `npm run check:process`, then bisected the chained scripts and read the bundle. | M | Yes for the shape — the idiom is common and bundling is the repo default for scripts. | **Fix shipped:** gate on the entry file's *basename* (`path.basename(process.argv[1]).startsWith("build-authoring-brief")`) instead of full-path identity — bundling preserves the importer's outfile name, so a bundled check never matches. **Method note worth keeping:** when a "check" mutates state, diff `git status` around the *whole* chain first to confirm, then bisect the chain — reading the scripts alone would never have found this, because every individual script is correct in isolation and the bug lives in how they are compiled together. **Generalizable rule:** a module that exports pure helpers *and* self-executes on import is only safe while nothing bundles it; prefer extracting shared helpers, or gate on something bundling cannot spoof. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-686 item 3.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-686, hourly pickup) — process-friction (S): a ticket's prescribed fix was unworkable against its own named example, and only checking the example caught it.** THR-686 item 2 specified scoping `lint:plan-doc` "to dated `Docs/plans/20??-??-??-*.md` files (or honour a frontmatter opt-out)" so that `systemic-wiring-guide.md` would be exempt. But the wiring guide's real filename is **`2026-04-16-systemic-wiring-guide.md`** — it *is* date-prefixed, so the primary suggestion would have left it linted and all 31 false findings intact, while the ticket would have read as satisfied. The two other files it named (`wiring-checklist.md`, `_template.md`) were **already** exempt via existing `PLAN_DOC_SKIP_PATTERNS`, so a filename-pattern approach would have shipped zero behaviour change and closed the ticket. Implemented the parenthetical option (frontmatter opt-out) instead. | ~3 min — cost only because the filename was checked against the proposal before coding. | S | Yes for the shape; ties directly to THR-688 (ticket-authoring rules), which is about tickets encoding snapshots that do not survive contact. | **Method:** before implementing a ticket's prescribed mechanism, run it against the ticket's own named example and confirm it produces the claimed result. **New 2026-07-21 (THR-674, hourly pickup) — tooling (S): `lint:plan-doc` lints `Docs/plans/.intent-proposals/*.md` as if they were plan docs, so salvaging gate artifacts emits a wall of false ERRORs.** Committing 4 recovered intent-proposal files produced ~40 advisory errors (`Missing required section heading: ## Engine pillar`, `## Constants table`, `## Fail-soft table`, `Missing three_pillars metadata block`, …). The lint is advisory so nothing was blocked, but the noise buries any genuine finding in the same run, which is the failure mode THR-686 item 2 was filed against for the wiring guide. Note the `.intent-proposals/` directory is *nested under* `Docs/plans/`, so any glob rooted at `Docs/plans/**` picks it up by default. | ~2 min — recognised as noise immediately, but each commit's output had to be scanned to confirm no real finding was hiding in it. | S | Yes — recurs on every commit that touches an intent-proposal, which is every design-session handoff. | **Fix:** add `.intent-proposals/` to `PLAN_DOC_SKIP_PATTERNS` in `scripts/lint-plan-doc.ts` (the same mechanism that already exempts `wiring-checklist.md` and `_template.md`), or give the directory the `> **lint_plan_doc:** exempt` frontmatter marker THR-686 added — the directory-level skip is preferable since it needs doing once rather than per-file. **Method note:** when a lint is scoped by directory glob, check for *nested* directories holding a different document type before trusting the glob. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-674 scope item 1 salvage.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-677, hourly pickup) — stale-reference (M): a "verbatim port" of a recovered prompt would have shipped two dead references, and only checking each claim against live state caught them.** THR-677's `daily-backlog-grooming` source prompt was recovered verbatim (a rare win — the Cowork task delivered its own instructions during a run, and they were pasted into the issue). The obvious move is to copy it across unchanged, since verbatim is precisely what the ticket asked for over guesswork. But two of its instructions were already dead: it opens Step 0 by querying `list_issues state:"In Review"`, and **`In Review` was retired 2026-06-23 by THR-487** (merge = Done) — `list_issue_statuses` confirms the team has no such state, so that query silently returns nothing every single day. Separately, `weekly-project-hygiene`'s on-disk prompt audited `.claude/skills/` vs `.agents/skills/` parity and the THR-192 sync hook, machinery **THR-654 demolished hours earlier on the same day**. Yes | Session: THR-677 hourly pickup, worktree focused-lamarr-43cc02

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-688, hourly pickup) — tooling (S): THR-686's `lint:plan-doc` date-glob scoping does not exempt *standing* docs that happen to carry a date prefix, so editing the coordination protocol emits 31 false ERRORs.** Committing a 3-file docs change fired the pre-commit hook's `lint:plan-doc --staged` against `Docs/plans/2026-04-13-linear-coordination-protocol.md` and produced 31 findings — `Missing ## Engine pillar`, `## Constants table`, `## Fail-soft table`, `Missing three_pillars metadata block`, and so on. **New 2026-07-21 (THR-689, hourly pickup) — testing (S): an engine test that "runs N ticks" has two invisible ceilings — the doom clock and vitest's 5s default — and the first one silently makes a correct guard-rail assertion false.** Writing the cap regression for `__DEBUG.tick(n)`, the natural assertion for `DEBUG_TICK_MAX = 200` is `expect(result.ticksRun).toBe(200)`. It failed at **185**: on seed 42 / `MAP_SIZE_PRESETS.small` the doom clock ends the run and the state leaves `phase: 'playing'` around tick 185, so the batch correctly stopped early and reported `stoppedReason: 'phase_left_playing'`. The implementation was right and the *test* was wrong — it had coupled a guard-rail assertion to doom-clock pacing. The failure reads like a cap-arithmetic bug, which is the trap: the obvious next move is to "fix" the clamp. Second ceiling, hit immediately after: ~185 real ticks takes **~8s**, over vitest's 5s per-test default, so the corrected test then timed out and needed an explicit `}, 60_000)`. | ~10 min across two red runs before the doom-clock ceiling was recognised as the cause rather than the clamp. | S | Yes | **Workaround:** for any test bounded by a tick count, assert the *guarantee* (`toBeLessThanOrEqual(CAP)`) rather than an exact count, and add an independent witness that the loop is bounded — here, a counting `resolveTargets` callback invoked once per attempted tick, which proves boundedness without depending on how far the sim actually got. Give any test running >~50 real ticks an explicit timeout. **Method note:** when a tick-count assertion fails just under its target, check `state.phase` before suspecting the bound — a run that legitimately ended is indistinguishable from a miscounted loop if you only look at the number. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-689 cap regression test.

**New 2026-07-21 (THR-691, hourly pickup) — tooling (M): GitHub's server-side merge ignores `.gitattributes` merge drivers entirely — including the *built-in* `union` — so a `merge=union` attribute cannot keep a PR out of `CONFLICTING`.** THR-691's scope reasoned that GitHub declines *custom* merge drivers (which require a local `git config merge.<name>.driver` GitHub cannot run) but might honour `union`, since it is built into git itself and needs no local configuration. Measured directly rather than assumed, per the handoff's explicit instruction: with `Docs/changelog.md merge=union` committed and live **on the base branch**, two branches appending different rows at the same line produced `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/merges` → **`409 Merge conflict`**, and an equivalent PR read **`mergeable: CONFLICTING`, `mergeStateStatus: DIRTY`** — the precise THR-668 symptom the attribute was meant to prevent. The same branch pair merges **clean (exit 0, both rows, header intact)** locally. Conclusion: GitHub's merge machinery does not consult `.gitattributes` at all; the built-in-vs-custom distinction is irrelevant to it. | The attribute delivers no GitHub-side benefit, so the web "Resolve conflicts" button and auto-merge remain unable to settle closeout-doc conflicts. Had this not been measured, the ticket would have shipped as a silent partial fix and the next idled PR would have gone CONFLICTING anyway, with a plausible-looking `.gitattributes` entry suggesting it should not have. | M | Yes | **Workaround (now documented, not rediscovered per-run):** resolve locally and push — `git fetch origin main && git merge origin/main && git push`. Union then auto-resolves the three closeout docs and the PR leaves CONFLICTING. Any claim that a merge attribute is load-bearing needs the A/B control with the attribute absent. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-691 union-merge verification.

**New 2026-07-22 (THR-692, hourly pickup) — tooling (M): armed auto-merge does not self-heal a `BEHIND` branch under strict branch protection, so an "arm and forget" PR can idle indefinitely with every check green.** Resuming THR-692 found PR #696 open ~10h after the prior run reported "auto-merge armed, CI green" — an accurate report. All required checks *were* `SUCCESS` (`Test · Typecheck · Build`, Vercel), auto-merge *was* enabled, and `mergeable` was `MERGEABLE` with **no conflict**. The blocker was `mergeStateStatus: BEHIND`: `main` had advanced two commits after the PR was armed, and branch protection runs in **strict mode** ("branches must be up to date before merging"), which this repo has had since THR-282. GitHub's auto-merge does *not* update a stale branch on its own unless the repo's "always suggest updating pull request branches" auto-update setting is on — it is not — so the PR sat waiting for a branch update no one was going to perform. This is a **distinct failure mode from impediment #135 and THR-691**, which both cover auto-merge stalling at `DIRTY`/`CONFLICTING` from append-only closeout-doc conflicts and are resolved by a local merge; here there is nothing to resolve, the branch is merely stale. A survey of the board found the class is not isolated: **9 of 15 open PRs carry auto-merge armed and unmerged**, the oldest from 2026-07-03 (#488), i.e. ~19 days of silent idling. | This run: ~5 min to diagnose, ~1 command to clear. Across the lane: unbounded — a PR in this state never merges and never reports failure, so its Linear issue never auto-closes and the next hourly run re-resumes an issue whose work is genuinely complete. | M | Yes | **Workaround:** `gh pr update-branch <N>` — a GitHub-side merge of the base into the head branch, no local tree needed and no worktree checkout required. It re-triggers CI; auto-merge then fires unattended once the required check is green. **Method note worth keeping:** `gh pr view --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus` returns **`UNKNOWN`/`UNKNOWN` on first call** — GitHub computes mergeability lazily and the first query only schedules the computation. A single call is therefore useless for this diagnosis; re-query until it resolves (2–3 calls, a few seconds apart) before concluding anything about a PR's mergeability. Reading the first `UNKNOWN` as "no information available" is what lets a `BEHIND` PR stay invisible. **Systemic fix worth a ticket:** the THR-675 "arm and move on" guidance is sound but incomplete — it needs either the repo's branch auto-update setting enabled (which makes "arm and forget" actually true), or a sweep that reconciles armed-but-unmerged PRs. Filed as THR-702, which also carries the 9-PR backlog for separate triage — most are `docs(plan): batch flush` artifacts from the `flush-plan-docs` task retired in THR-654 and may be obsolete rather than wanted, so they need a per-PR call rather than a bulk merge. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-692 resume.

**Recurrence 2026-07-22 (THR-696, hourly pickup) — tooling (S): the `BEHIND`-at-arm-time case fires on a *freshly opened* PR, not only on one that idled.** THR-702 documents armed auto-merge stalling at `mergeStateStatus: BEHIND` after a PR sits and `main` advances. This run hit it on a PR that was **seconds old**: the branch was verified at `origin/main` tip immediately before the work started (`git rev-list HEAD..origin/main --count` → 0), but `main` moved during the session, so `gh pr merge --auto --merge` armed straight into `BEHIND`. Cheap containment, already applied here: after arming, read `gh pr view <n> --json autoMergeRequest,mergeStateStatus,mergeable` **once** and run `gh pr update-branch` if the state is `BEHIND` — one extra call, no CI polling, and it moves the PR to `BLOCKED`/`MERGEABLE` (check pending) which auto-merge *can* resolve unattended. This strengthens THR-702's case: the fix belongs in the closeout path unconditionally, not as an idle-PR remedy, because branch-tip freshness at session start says nothing about freshness at arm time.

**Resolved 2026-07-24 (next hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, resuming THR-722).** The flake was not cosmetic: it is the *only* thing that failed CI on PR #779, so the armed auto-merge could never fire and THR-722 sat shipped-but-unmergeable. Fixed by passing `MILESTONE_SMOKE_TIMEOUT_MS` (already defined in the file) to the second `it`, pushed onto the PR branch. Full suite then went **866 files / 12982 tests, 0 failures** — the first fully-green local suite recorded in this log, which means the "1 known pre-existing failure" baseline everyone had been quoting *was* this flake and nothing else.

**Two lessons worth more than the one-line fix.** (1) **This is a recurrence of #142** — same file, same root cause, 6 weeks apart. THR-293's fix added `MILESTONE_SMOKE_TIMEOUT_MS` to the `it.each` block and left the plain `it` below it on the 5s default; that second test runs **40 ticks** (30 + 10) versus the parametrised one's 30, so the *slower* test was the one left unguarded. When adding a timeout to one test in a file, grep the whole file for sibling `it(`/`it.each(` calls doing comparable work. (2) **"Pre-existing, not mine" is a correct diagnosis but an incomplete action.** The prior run proved pre-existence rigorously and then shipped anyway with auto-merge armed — which cannot merge past a red required check, so the ticket silently stalled for an hour. Cheaper still when the workflow's effect is observable in a system of record — here the Linear `stateHistory` array (`endedAt: null` on a single entry) proved "never transitioned" independently of the log, and its `completedAt` matched the ✅ line to the second, which is stronger evidence than either source alone. **General rule: prefer the state the workflow changed over the log of it changing.** | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-738 live verification.

**New 2026-07-25 (hourly pickup) — environment (Blocked): GitHub Actions stopped executing jobs on an account-billing failure, which both stranded a finished ticket and silently opened the merge gate. Resume the ticket, comment the evidence, unassign to free the WIP slot, exit clean. **After restore:** a startup-failed run is never retriggered by anything, so each stranded ticket needs its auto-close run re-run by hand (for THR-731, run `30162937429`) or the issue closed manually. **Durable fix, now recommended for the third time (#136 proposed it in May and it was never built):** a billing-failure detector on the hourly tick that greps `gh run list` output for the account-payment string, surfaces it as a Christian-facing item, and exits clean — this class is trivially machine-detectable and has now cost three separate sessions the same rediscovery. **RESOLVED 2026-07-25 ~18:00 UTC (next hourly run).** Billing was restored between runs; the proof is a *fresh* run executing jobs, not a signature — THR-732's PR #856 ran `Test · Typecheck · Build` for 17 minutes (17:39:25→17:56:55Z) and passed, versus the 3–5s zero-job deaths. **New 2026-07-25 (THR-732, hourly pickup) — engineering (M): the plan's named input for Reunite was a property that dissolution deliberately empties, so the verb would have found nobody to call.** The THR-732 plan specifies Reunite's targets as "living un-grouped **roster** members" of a disbanded company, and its Substrate Honesty table verifies the backing shape as *"Disbanded-company persistence (`groupStatus: 'disbanded'`, `roster`, `disbandedAtTick`) — Yes, `groupQueries.ts`, persisted by `dissolveGroup`."* Both halves of that check are true and the conclusion is still wrong: `dissolveGroup` **sets `roster: []`** on its way out. The property exists on disbanded companies, is documented, is persisted — and is always empty on exactly the input Reunite takes. A faithful implementation returns zero gatherable members for every target, forever, and the failure is silent: the eligibility predicate simply never passes, so the card is never offered and no error is raised. What actually survives dissolution is the **`member_of` edges**, which `dissolveGroup` stamps with `leftAtTick` rather than removing — and `groupDissolution.ts`'s own file header says so in as many words ("that pair is the historical record prose reads from later"). | ~15 min, caught while reading `dissolveGroup` to confirm the window property would not be clobbered — i.e. by reading the producer, not the consumer. | M | Yes — any feature that reads a "historical" property off an entity its own lifecycle code tears down. | **Workaround:** a `getFormerGroupMembers` query that walks *all* incoming `member_of` edges including the closed ones, with `getReunitableMembers` layering the living/ungrouped filter on top; the interface-map row for it names the mechanism as the `leftAtTick` **edge property** written by `dissolveGroup`, not the accessor function, so the contract points at the thing that actually crosses the boundary. **The generalisable check:** Step 0.6 asks *does this substrate exist* — for anything read after an entity's death, the follow-up question is **"what does the teardown path do to it?"** Grepping the property name finds the declaration and the writer and tells you it is real; only reading the *destructor* tells you it is empty when you need it. Both a roster-based and an edge-based implementation pass a naive "returns former members" test written against a live company — the discriminating fixture has to dissolve the group first, which is why the shipped test asserts `roster === []` and the edge-walk returning all three riders **in the same test body**. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-732.

The engine's spheres are `force / matter / energy / life / mind / spirit / time / entropy` plus the four Foundation spheres — **only `mind` and `spirit` appear in both sets**, so six of that pool's eight keys are unreachable content, silently absorbed by its `?? []` fallback. The invented id surfaced not through any action-template test but through `ascendantBeatPresentation.test.tsx`, which renders every milestone beat and its granted cards: `SPHERE_COLORS['dusk']` returned `undefined` and `tintDark` died on `hex.slice(1)`. The authoritative sets here are `SPHERE_COLORS` / `REACH_TO_SPHERE` in `src/components/icons/constants.ts`. **Worth noting how it was caught:** a sweep test that renders every member of a registry (here, every milestone beat *with its granted cards*) turned an invented data value into a hard failure at the UI layer, which no data-shape test would have done — `sphereAffinity` is typed `SphereName`, and `'dusk'` only failed to compile because the union is real; had the field been `string`, the crash would have waited for a player to open the beat modal. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-732.

**New 2026-07-25 (THR-734, hourly pickup) — process (S): a handoff instruction went stale between authoring and pickup, and following it faithfully would have written drift into the artifact that exists to prevent drift.** THR-734's handoff (2026-07-24) split its five terms into "shipped — reconcile against code" (Group, Company, Group Cohesion) and "design-approved, not yet shipped (THR-74 PR 2b) — add with the not-yet-implemented marker" (Draw Together, Bless this Company). **New 2026-07-25 (THR-734 resume, hourly pickup) — environment (S): an armed, fully-green PR sat unmerged because auto-merge does not refresh a stale branch, and the freshening then surfaced a Vercel deploy blackout that looks like a merge blocker and is not.** Two separate things, both worth writing down because the second is the one that costs time. **(1) The stale-branch half is the known THR-702 class**: PR #859 (THR-734) was opened, armed, and passed `Test · Typecheck · Build` in 17m57s — then `main` moved and the PR went `mergeStateStatus: BEHIND`, where strict branch protection holds it silently and forever. `gh pr update-branch 859` cleared it in one command. This is exactly what pull-work Step 0.8 exists to catch, and it worked as designed on the first hourly run after the ship — the entry is here to record that the sweep's *value* is real and measured, not hypothetical: without it the ticket idles In Dev holding the WIP=1 slot while being entirely finished. **(2) The new half:** freshening the branch re-ran the checks, and `Vercel` now reports `fail` with *"Deployment rate limited — retry in 24 hours"* (link: `vercel.com/spliid?upgradeToPro=build-rate-limit`) — an account-level build rate limit, not a repo defect. Production deploys had been landing normally until `76ab4af6` at 18:03Z; 22 GitHub-registered deployments (12 Production, 10 Preview) in the preceding 23h. **The trap is that a red `Vercel` X on an armed PR reads exactly like a merge blocker.** It is not: `gh api repos/.../branches/main/protection` returns `required_status_checks.contexts == ["Test · Typecheck · Build"]` — Vercel is *not* a required check, so a Vercel failure cannot stop auto-merge. | ~10 min, all of it in the second half — deciding whether the red X blocked the ship. | S | Yes for both halves — (1) recurs on every PR whose base moves before it merges, which is most of them in an hourly lane; (2) recurs for the whole 24h window and on any future limit hit. | **Workaround / posture:** (1) run the Step 0.8 sweep before anything else and `gh pr update-branch` the oldest `BEHIND` PR — one per run, since each merge re-stales the rest. Note `mergeStateStatus` reads `UNKNOWN` on first query (GitHub computes it lazily) and `BLOCKED` immediately after an update-branch (checks re-running, auto-merge still armed) — neither means "broken", so do not act on the first read. (2) **Do not treat a red `Vercel` check as a merge gate — query the protection rule instead of inferring from the checks list.** `gh api repos/christianspliid-ui/threadbare/branches/main/protection --jq '.required_status_checks.contexts'` is the authoritative answer and costs one call; the checks list mixes required and advisory contexts with no visual distinction. **Real consequence to expect, though:** while the limit holds, a merge to `main` will not produce a fresh production deploy, so the Definition-of-Done "Deploy" step is satisfied-on-paper only. Christian-facing if it persists past the 24h window (resolution is a plan decision, no agent action clears it); self-resolving otherwise, which is why this is logged rather than filed as an issue. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, 2026-07-25 ~19:30 UTC; THR-734 resume.

**New 2026-07-26 (THR-736, hourly pickup) — engineering (M): a *required* interface field was missing from 18 shipped objects and `tsc` reported nothing, because those literals already fail assignability on a different property.** THR-736's premise was that `actorAffinities` (declared `readonly actorAffinities: readonly ActorType[]` — required, no `?`) was absent from 18 templates and survived only because the red typecheck baseline (THR-489) hides it inside the pre-existing error mass, so fixing it would show a **decrease**. The first half is right and the second is wrong in an instructive way: the ratchet held at **3519 unchanged**, with per-file counts identical before and after (`mercenary-encounter-content.ts` 46, `effect-shell-proof-templates.ts` 7). These literals carry property-level errors (`reach: 'resolve'` / `'combat'` are not `ReachDomain` members), and TypeScript reports those mismatches rather than emitting a separate missing-property diagnostic — the same masking hides absent `apCost` and `crudType` on the proof pack, neither of which is optional either. A guard that dies exactly when it starts mattering is worse than no guard, because it reads as coverage. Same vacuity class as THR-731 PR 4's `sublocationTypes` check. (2) **Falsify it before trusting it** — deleting one field and confirming the failure names `encounter.shell_proof.fate_card_trial` took two minutes; a first falsification attempt silently no-opped (the replace anchor didn't match) and *passed*, which is precisely the false confidence the practice exists to catch. **The generalisable read for Done-whens:** a predicted gate movement is a hypothesis about a tool's behavior, not an acceptance criterion. When the gate disagrees with the ticket, measure the gate's own output per-file with and without the change before assuming either side — and when the type system turns out never to have enforced a "required" field, say so in the closeout rather than reaching for `--update` to manufacture the predicted delta. | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-736.

It was recoverable in seconds (re-run the insert script) and nothing shipped wrong, but it silently undid completed work, and the same reflex on an unscripted hand-edit would have cost the whole file. Compounded by the fact that the falsification itself had no-opped, so the run proved nothing *and* destroyed the edits. | ~5 min. | S | Yes — any falsify-the-guard cycle, which is now standard practice after THR-731 PR 4. | **Workaround:** never use `git checkout --` as the undo for a deliberate temporary mutation of a file you have already edited — it has no concept of "just my last change". Copy the file to a scratch path first (`cp <file> /tmp/<name>.bak`) and restore with `cp` back, which is exact regardless of what else is uncommitted; verify with a cheap positive check afterwards (`grep -c actorAffinities <file>` → expected count) rather than assuming the restore worked. **The sharper lesson is to make the mutation impossible to confuse with real work:** prefer falsifying against a temporary *copy* of the registry, or commit the real edits first so `git checkout --` genuinely means "discard only the experiment." | Hourly `tb-opus-pickup` run, THR-736.

**New 2026-07-26 (THR-780, hourly pickup) — environment (M): a true 1920×1080 viewport was unobtainable from *either* browser surface in this headless run — the two failure modes are complementary, so neither can cover for the other.** The DoD's Browser-verify bullet asks for a screenshot at the contractual 1920×1080. **Browser pane:** `resize_window` worked exactly — `innerWidth/innerHeight` read `1920x1080` — but `computer{action:"screenshot"}` failed in 5s with `the Browser pane is not displayed, so the page is not compositing frames`, on both the WebGL game view and after the sim was paused. A pane that is never displayed in a scheduled run cannot produce pixels at any viewport. **Claude-in-Chrome:** screenshots fine (captured the live WebGL hex map with 425 agents), but its viewport is **pinned at 1430×989** and does not follow `resize_window` — requesting 1920×1080 gave 1430×989, and over-requesting 2410×1171 to compensate for browser chrome *also* gave 1430×989, on a 3440×1440 screen with room to spare (the tab appears constrained by a side-panel layout, and `outerWidth/outerHeight` read `0x0` from the extension context). So one surface has the right viewport and no pixels; the other has pixels and the wrong viewport. This is the exact class THR-754 exists to codify, and it extends impediment #185/#199: the previous entries record the Browser-pane hang and the pure-DOM case, but not that the Chrome fallback *silently ignores the resize* — which matters because a screenshot taken there looks valid and is quietly off-contract. | The literal 1920×1080 artifact could not be produced for a correct change; ~10 min spent proving both surfaces were dead ends rather than assuming one. | M | Yes | **Workaround:** report the real captured viewport rather than implying the contractual one, and carry the load-bearing evidence in assertions instead of pixels — here a `__DEBUG`-driven state assertion (tally delta, per-effect trace counts) plus a *phase-attributed* console capture, with the screenshot demoted to "surface still renders, no visual regression". Always print `innerWidth`/`innerHeight` in the same call as the screenshot; `resize_window` reporting success is not evidence the viewport changed. **Durable fix:** THR-754 covered the Browser-pane and pure-DOM halves; the Claude-in-Chrome half was closed separately by THR-796 (2026-07-27), which proved the resize is *inert* rather than *pinned* — see the entry below. | THR-780 aftermath StrictMode fix, browser-verify pass. |

**New 2026-07-26 (THR-780, hourly pickup) — engineering (M): "the console has errors" was about to be attributed to my change, and only a phase-split plus a live pre/post A/B showed the errors were pre-existing and the *real* metric had a clean 2×→1× signature.** Browser-verifying the aftermath fix, the console showed four `Encountered two children with the same key` errors. That last step doubled as the strongest evidence in the closeout: pre-fix `delta: 2` / 2 applied-traces / 4 effect-traces vs post-fix `delta: 1` / 1 / 2, same seed, same agent, same reaction. | THR-780 aftermath StrictMode fix, browser-verify pass. |

**New 2026-07-26 (THR-780, hourly pickup) — process-friction (S): CLAUDE.md documents the home-tree `node_modules` health probe as a path that does not exist in this install, so following the doc literally reports catastrophic damage on a perfectly healthy tree.** CLAUDE.md's § Scheduled Tasks says `check_home_node_modules` "verifies `node_modules/.bin/esbuild.exe` still exists". Running exactly that at closeout printed `DAMAGED` — the THR-753 wipe signature, which is alarming enough to derail a closeout. The tree was fine: 284 packages, `vitest` present, `@esbuild/win32-x64/esbuild.exe` present.
